lesson.title: The Vinegar and Baking Soda Reaction, Explained: Acid-Carbonate Reactions
lesson.summary: When an acid reacts with a carbonate or bicarbonate, it produces a salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas, the same fizzing chemistry behind baking soda volcanoes, antacid tablets, and field tests for limestone.
lesson.body:
Acid-carbonate reactions are the most common specific example of a gas evolution reaction, so common that it is worth learning the pattern by name: acid plus metal carbonate yields a salt, plus water, plus carbon dioxide gas, and the same pattern holds for bicarbonates too. The mechanism follows directly from what you already know: the acid donates a proton to the carbonate ion, forming carbonic acid, H2CO3, which is too unstable to exist for long and decomposes almost immediately into water and CO2 gas, the gas that then escapes and drives the reaction to completion.

Work through a fully verified example using calcium carbonate, the compound that makes up limestone, chalk, and eggshells, reacting with hydrochloric acid: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) is right arrow CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g). Check the atoms carefully. Calcium: 1 on each side. Carbon: 1 on each side. Oxygen: 3 on the left, all from CaCO3, matching 1 from H2O plus 2 from CO2, or 3, on the right. Hydrogen: 2 on the left from 2HCl, matching 2 on the right from H2O. Chlorine: 2 on each side. Every element balances. This exact reaction is also why acid rain and even dilute vinegar slowly eat away at limestone buildings and marble statues over time, visibly bubbling as the stone dissolves.

The kitchen version of this reaction is just as easy to verify. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, and vinegar is a dilute aqueous solution of acetic acid: NaHCO3(aq) + CH3COOH(aq) is right arrow CH3COONa(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g). Check the atoms. Sodium: 1 equals 1. Hydrogen: 1 from NaHCO3 plus 4 from CH3COOH gives 5 on the left, matching 3 from CH3COONa plus 2 from H2O, or 5, on the right. Carbon: 1 plus 2 gives 3 on the left, matching 2 plus 1, or 3, on the right. Oxygen: 3 plus 2 gives 5 on the left, matching 2 plus 1 plus 2, or 5, on the right. Fully balanced, atom for atom. As with the gas evolution reaction in the last chapter, this is not a redox reaction either, since no atom's oxidation number changes, it is purely an acid-base proton transfer followed by decomposition of the resulting carbonic acid. Keeping that distinction clear matters, since this unit covers both redox chemistry and this separate reaction family side by side.

This chemistry shows up well beyond the kitchen. Antacid tablets often contain a carbonate or bicarbonate that fizzes on contact with stomach acid, neutralizing it while releasing harmless CO2 gas. Field geologists carry small bottles of dilute hydrochloric acid for exactly this reaction: a drop of acid that produces vigorous fizzing on a rock sample is a fast, reliable field test for carbonate minerals like calcite.
